extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners and students, internal/employee communication professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing and managing internal (employee) communication and internal relations within organizations, including cultural, legal, and change-management considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a strong manager communication network
rubrics_metrics.description: Make every supervisor at every level accountable for communicating effectively with his or her employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This communication should be more than just job-related information and should include key business and public issues affecting the total organization. Managers are responsible for two-way interactive communications as a way-of-life throughout the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize effective two-way communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective, two-way communication is the foundation for management–employee relations and overall job performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations that do not prioritize two-way communication lose human resource potential and risk behaviors summarized as 'slothing on the job' (absenteeism, grievances, poor quality, withheld effort and ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations as coordinator/mediator for internal relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations staff, with communication knowledge and skills, should coordinate and mediate employee relations and be central to managing internal relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practitioners often facilitate communication between management and employees and may play a key role in resolving internal conflicts and shaping communication strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a climate of trust and honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective employee communication develops in a climate of trust and honesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Day-to-day working relationships involve heavy contact, but communication succeeds only when trust and honesty prevail. The chief executive must establish and endorse this culture as formal policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven conditions of effective working relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Working relationships ideally are characterized by: (1) confidence and trust between employer and employees; (2) honest, candid information flowing up, down, and sideways; (3) satisfying status and participation for each person; (4) continuity of work without strife; (5) healthy or safe surroundings; (6) success for the enterprise; (7) optimism about the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions describe the desired climate for internal relations and serve as evaluative benchmarks for internal communication efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face-to-face communication and open-door policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Face-to-face communication with an 'open-door policy' is the primary medium for encouraging upward, two-way communication and building good working relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use face-to-face for listening and building relationships; prefer it for debate, clarification, and private feedback rather than for information-dumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance employee satisfaction with enterprise success
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal relations should balance the needs for employee satisfaction with the success of the enterprise as part of continuous adjustment and reconciliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal relations aim to establish and maintain mutually beneficial relationships between the organization and employees whose support determines success or failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for organizational culture in communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand organizational culture (shared meanings, values, symbols, beliefs, norms) because it significantly impacts the model of public relations practiced and internal communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poor cultural fit can make highly qualified employees ineffective; communication must work with an organization’s culture and worldview to be successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hofstede — Power-distance (message tailoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power-distance is the extent to which people see inequities as natural; affects whether managers and employees view themselves as different or equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In high power-distance organizations, communications may emphasize authority of top managers; in low power-distance settings, emphasize manager–employee similarities (e.g., CEOs interacting via blogs). Examples: South Korea (high), many U.S. corporations (low).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hofstede — Individualism vs collectivism (message framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individualism measures whether people put individual needs before group needs and influences whether rewards and messages focus on individual achievement or team responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In individualistic cultures emphasize individual actions and recognition; in collectivist cultures emphasize team benefits and shared responsibility. Employees from high-individualism cultures may prefer less standardization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hofstede — Uncertainty avoidance (structure preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty avoidance explains preference for communication and structures that reduce social anxiety (clear rules and instructions vs tolerance for ambiguity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High uncertainty avoidance favors clear requirements, rules, and less risk-taking; low uncertainty avoidance tolerates ambiguity and is more open to two-way public relations and input from the environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hofstede — Masculinity (value orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Masculinity describes preference for traditionally 'masculine' traits (competitiveness, aggressiveness) versus 'feminine' traits (nurturing, cooperation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In high-masculinity organizations, communication programs may use competition-based incentives; in low-masculinity organizations, emphasize how actions nurture employees’ self-esteem and cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open vs closed systems (organizational openness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations can be open systems (receive environmental input and adapt) or closed systems (do not receive input and resist adaptation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An organization’s openness affects internal communication: open systems encourage feedback and adaptation; closed systems resist external input and change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetrical vs asymmetrical worldviews
rubrics_metrics.description: An asymmetrical worldview seeks organizational goals without changing internal behavior (resists sharing power); a symmetrical worldview values negotiation, compromise, and adopting others' views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetrical worldviews are aligned with open systems and two-way dialogue; asymmetrical worldviews align with closed systems and centralized decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritarian organizational culture (communication characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authoritarian cultures arise from asymmetrical worldviews: structured, formalized communication within a decision-making hierarchy, centralized decisions, little input sought from lower levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication is one-sided (management-to-employee), feedback is minimal and unlikely to change decisions, efficiency is valued over innovation, and such cultures resist change—leading to higher turnover and lower job satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participative organizational culture (communication characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participative cultures arise from symmetrical worldviews: value dialogue and exchange, teamwork, decentralization, and input from employees and stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feedback is sought and taken seriously, innovation is encouraged, departments are integrated, decision-making is decentralized, and employees at all levels can influence outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-acculturation in multinational organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-acculturation: simultaneous orientation toward each other’s cultures in multinational settings; applied via three key measures—agreement, congruency, and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improve co-acculturation agreement (shared evaluations), congruency (own view vs estimate of other group's view), and accuracy (correct estimation of other group’s perceptions) to enhance employee communication in diverse organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate safety and legal compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal relations must ensure employees know and follow governing standards (country-specific regulations such as taxes, labor laws, workplace safety, environmental laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal relations educate employees about compliance (OSHA, EPA examples), display required posters, maintain monitoring (e.g., benzene alarms), and communicate safety-critical information—responsible communication can be a matter of life and death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor relations and union communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain continuous, proactive communication with unionized and nonunionized hourly employees; internal relations often handle early signals of discontent and are responsible for communicating about dissension and resolving problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HR handles hiring/training/benefits, but internal relations must facilitate labor–management relationships, manage strike risks, and accord attention to nonunionized labor as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicating organizational change (three-phase approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a three-phase approach during change: Phase 1 acknowledge passing of the old and celebrate the new; Phase 2 cognitive restructuring (timing critical for denial/resistance/exploration); Phase 3 commitment (reward, training, validation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives: reduce fear and uncertainty, limit rumors, restore control, maintain morale, and increase knowledge of assistance for displaced workers. Timing and honesty are critical; employees want practical answers about jobs, locations, reasons, improvements, and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and timely disclosure during change
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal relations should be forthright and expedient when communicating change; truthful information builds trust and reduces rumor and speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide factual information rapidly; 'We are still working that out' is better than 'No comment.' Push management to be honest with employees even when information is unfavorable (Enron cited as a negative example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose communication media appropriately during change
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer face-to-face communication for debate, clarifying understanding, and private feedback; use email, newsletters, and intranet for raising awareness and sharing information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using impersonal channels for 'information dumping'—reserve them for awareness-building and save interpersonal methods for two-way interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal communication purposes (fourfold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal communication serves to acculturate employees, inform them of organizational developments, listen to their concerns, and foster employee-to-employee communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New technologies affect delivery, but the purposes remain: help employees internalize culture/values, provide consistent messaging (internal/external congruence), and enable listening mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vision statement design and function
rubrics_metrics.description: A vision statement represents a future goal and answers 'Why does this organization exist?' and 'What would we like to accomplish?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vision statements help manage reactions to environmental change, articulate values and strategic priorities, and are typically created by top leadership—though involving employees can foster shared vision and ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission statement design and function
rubrics_metrics.description: A mission statement answers 'How are we different from our competitors?' and conveys goals, structure, legitimacy, values, participation, leadership, ethical priorities, and commitment to stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mission statements are more specific and operational than vision statements and help employees set priorities and stay 'on strategy'; top-performing organizations typically have clear vision and mission statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage employees in vision/mission creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Involving employees in creating vision and mission statements fosters pride, ownership, and responsibility and helps create a shared vision throughout the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating vision/mission solely at the top risks missing employee engagement; participatory development promotes buy-in and clearer internalization of organizational values.
